query: Consider the following context: Noble metal–based high-entropy alloys (NM-HEAs) are promising catalysts because of their diverse compositions and complex surface structures, although understanding their formation and achieving precise atomic control remain challenging. In that context, which method can be used for produce HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks, and why?

generation.hypothesis: The formation of HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks can be achieved through a method that utilizes the cocktail effect and the high entropy effect to create a solid-solution structure with face-centered cubic (FCC) and body-centered cubic (BCC) lattices.
generation.material_initial_state: Noble metal-based high-entropy alloys (NM-HEAs) with diverse compositions and complex surface structures
generation.intervention: Utilization of the cocktail effect and the high entropy effect to create a solid-solution structure
generation.conditions: Equal or near-equal atomic ratios of five or more metals, high configurational entropy, and low atomic diffusion
generation.structural_mediator: Face-centered cubic (FCC) and body-centered cubic (BCC) lattices
generation.mechanism: The cocktail effect and the high entropy effect lead to the formation of a solid-solution structure, resulting in enhanced reactivity and stability
generation.predicted_outcome: The formation of HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks with high structural stability and potential for catalytic applications
generation.baseline: Traditional superalloys with limited high-temperature strength and stability
generation.boundary: The limitations of traditional superalloys and the need for new materials with high-temperature strength and stability
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of the cocktail effect and the high entropy effect on the formation of HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks, and the potential applications of these materials

falsification_experiment.design: In situ aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles
measurements: Structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental results show no significant structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text:
First reported in 2004 [ [1] ], high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys comprising five or more elements in equal or nearly equal molar fractions, with each element present at a mole fraction of approximately 5–35 at.% [ [2] ]. The presence of multiple elements leads to a high configurational entropy, resulting in solid-solution structures with face-centred cubic (FCC) and body-centred cubic (BCC) lattices, rather than intermetallic compounds [ [3] ]. In recent years, HEAs have garnered significant consideration in the field of materials science because of their exceptional performance characteristics, including high strength [ [4] ], corrosion resistance [ [5] ], soft magnetic properties [ [6] ], high hardness [ [7] ], wear resistance [ [8] ], fatigue resistance [ [9] ], and softening resistance at high temperatures [ [10] ]. The superior high-temperature behaviour of HEAs can be attributed to four underlying effects: the high entropy effect, the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect, the severe lattice distortion effect, and the cocktail effect [ [11] ].

To extend the potential of nanoalloys in different fields such as catalysis or mechanics, much attention has recently been paid to multi‐element nanoparticles (NPs), also known as high‐entropy nanoalloys (HENA), which consist of nanostructures composed of five or more metals, in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios, crystallized in a solid solution. [ [1] ] Although many physical and chemical fabrication methods have been developed [ [2] ] there are still many gray areas concerning the synthesis‐structure‐properties relationships in these complex nanomaterials. The synergy of several effects makes HENA potentially efficient and stable nano‐catalysts: the “cocktail” effect due to the interaction between the different elements can give rise to enhanced reactivity which counterbalances the low content of noble metals in the nanostructure. The variety of elements and atomic sizes generate many lattice distortions and crystalline defects that can create preferential surface reaction sites.
